story_text.value:
ChamberZero has been a long-running personal project. This launch includes a complete redesign of the site and integration of election finance data.

A complete money universe is constructed directly from itemized FEC transactions, 2008 to today.

Elections go all the way back to 1788; who won every seat, with vote counts since 1976 (presidential since 1828).

Bills, actions, and other legislative metadata go back to 1975 and roll-call votes to 1989 (as far as the public sources go).

The Miller-column style allows quick drilling down to the raw source backing aggregate claims, especially useful for political data.

For example [1]:

Texas Elections → Talarico vs. Paxton → His top individual donor at $44.5K, well over the per-person limit → which turns out to be $63K given to the Talarico Victory Fund, with only Talarico's share credited to him → Each check linked to the FEC filing it was reported on.

[1] https://chamberzero.com/col/home/elections-overview%3Acurren...

title.value: Show HN: U.S. Elections, Campaign Finance and Legislation on a Miller-Column UI

story_text.value:
The linked repo is 100% vibe coded, but it was built on a handful of principles:

- Most tax software derives trust from the party who maintains it (e.g. Intuit, the IRS, etc.) - Vibe coded software lacks this trustworthiness. - Therefore any formalization should build in verifiability and mechanisms that make it possible for users/maintainers to trace claims/interpretations back to authoritative source documents.

It's very much a back-burner passive project right now (do not use this for anything real!), but I feel strongly that something like this ought to exist for the public good. I built it to get a sense of what the shape of what such a thing might be.

story_text.value:
I built this because I tried many sales tax APIs and the problems were: a) the rates were a black box with no source attached b) lookups resolved by ZIP code.

ZIP codes are postal routes, not tax jurisdictions. Stripe's Tax team wrote a good post on this [1]: two houses in Drexel, MO share a city, a ZIP, and nearly a house number, but sit in different counties with different rates. If your lookup key is the ZIP, you are wrong on those addresses, even when the rate table is accurate.

OpenTaxRate resolves the street address instead: - SST member states (24): the quarterly rate + boundary files, street ranges and ZIP+4, not just the rate tables - Non-SST states: a custom adapter for each state, using its DOR's own published tables and boundary files (TX Comptroller, FL DR-15DSS, ALDOR, IDOR, NY Pub 718, California via CDTFA's lookup, etc) - Census TIGER for geometry

I tried with multiple open source geocoders you can self-host: Nominatim, Photon and Pelias, as well as proprietary ones (HERE, Geocodio, Mapbox, Google). Proprietary ones have higher accuracy, ~99.3% correct vs. 97.1% with just open source.

For comparison: Avalara AvaTax 99.6%, TaxJar 98.2%. Public benchmark set are in the repo and at opentaxrate.com/benchmarks.

Rates are just one part of sales tax, but also there's a ton of work in maintaining it as rules change. It doesn't handle exemptions, holidays, and caps.

It returns the rate, plus the state's own location and jurisdiction codes for the address, resolved to the address, with its official source attached. MIT licensed, you can self-host with Postgres + PostGIS.

[1]: https://stripe.dev/blog/how-we-built-it-jurisdiction-resolut...

story_text.value:
As my first experiment in AI autonomy, I set up an agent that runs the product, while I assist it. The product is the community board hosted on the homepage of 42Loop.com

On Product Development front, the agent ideates with me the features, positioning, UX etc. and provides me the prompts that I pass on to a coding agent (as we progress the goal is to take myself out of the loop)

On the marketing and ops front, the agent finds apps to list, reviews them, finds opportunities to promote the product across the web etc.

The agent and I communicate via the open boardroom here. It posts a daily briefing, I provide feedback. The goal for the agent is to hillclimb on the registered users metric.

Happy to answer anything about the setup. Looking for inputs and suggestions. The agent is reading as well. Thanks.

story_text.value:
Knowledge hits you from everywhere - papers, lectures, podcasts, chats - and most of it is gone by Friday, unless you give it a home.

MindForger - thinking notebook - is not intuitive as I build it mostly for myself, but my wife :) had a nice idea to explain what MindForger is about without a wall of text with a comic! It follows one knowledge junkie from the chaos of browser tabs and sticky notes, through typed notes, outlines, notebooks and shelves, Kanban and the Eisenhower matrix, private AI and finding what he wrote weeks ago, all the way to a thinking notebook that is private, free and his.

Enjoy!

story_text.value: I run Blockchain IQ. We sell some crypto data to software agents per request over x402 (HTTP 402, USDC on Base, no account or API key). In October we paid for integrations: 22 were submitted and we checked each one by matching its on-chain payment to our purchase log and running it in a clean temporary folder with a throwaway wallet. Twenty passed; the post lists all of them with the exact commits we ran. To try the API: `curl -i https://www.blockchainiq.co/api/x402/v1/brief` returns the 402 with the price ($0.01), and a wallet's first call is free. Questions about how we checked the code or what failed are welcome.
